name: PT. Mitra Adiperkasa Tbk

frontmatter.title: Mitra Adiperkasa: a store-led franchise priced for a broken consumer
frontmatter.summary: MAP is Indonesia's largest multi-brand lifestyle retailer, growing net revenue by a quarter in 2026 while retail sales growth slows to under one percent. A new controlling consortium bought control at a premium and tendered above the market; the shares trade far below both. We value the fundamentals at Rp1,786 and apply the konglo lens for the thin float, giving a target of Rp1,445.
thesis: Net revenue grew about a quarter in the first nine months of 2026 while Bank Indonesia's retail index grew 0.6% year on year in September: MAP is taking share, not riding a cycle.

At Rp1,210 the market pays 2.8x FY2026E EBITDA and 7.8x FY2026E earnings, the EBITDA multiple struck on the forecast net debt and the book minority while the P/E carries no leverage deduction, for a business earning 17.4% ROE on a lease-light equity base.
The new controller (Pacific Universal with CVC) bought the block at Rp1,395 and tendered at Rp1,550, both above the market; the shares have since fallen below both [S3].
Fundamental value is Rp1,786; the konglo lens keeps only part of that gap for a year because the float is thin and the free-float deadlines fall inside the window, hence Rp1,445 and ADD.
The bear case is a consumer recession plus a lease book that does not flex: retail growth is barely positive while MAP adds stores.

catalysts.event: MAPI leaves the LQ45 and IDX80 after the HSC list of 11 November
FTSE Russell deletes MAPI from its global indices at the December review, effective at the open
First free-float deadline: the first step up must be reached from about eleven and a half percent
MSCI decides on Indonesia Standalone status, the binding regime event for the complex

blocks.text: **ADD, target Rp1,445, total return 20.7%.** Our fundamental twelve-month value is Rp1,786 a share; the konglo lens then discounts that by the part of the price-to-value gap the float and the index calendar are likely to keep for another year, which lands the target at Rp1,445. The rating is a statement about the business first and the regime second: MAP earned IDR2,231.2bn of net profit on IDR43,083.2bn of revenue in FY2025, is running ahead of that in 2026, and trades at 7.8x FY2026E earnings and 2.8x EBITDA, that multiple struck on the FY2026E forecast net debt and the book minority rather than on the heavier 30 September balance sheet the valuation deducts [S0][S4].

Three things produce the return. First, the operating momentum is real and not a base effect: net revenue rose 24.5% in the first nine months of 2026 to IDR37.44tn, with the third quarter alone up 26.7% on the top line and nine-month net profit up 25.1%, while Bank Indonesia's retail sales index grew only 0.6% year on year in September and fell -3.1% month on month after the Independence Day normalisation [S4][S6]. Second, the balance sheet the valuation deducts is dated 30 September 2026 and is heavier than the FY2025A close: bank loans of IDR3,356.0bn, lease liabilities of IDR5,243.6bn and IDR1,908.9bn of Sports Direct Malaysia consideration still payable, against IDR4,939.5bn of cash and IDR1,024.4bn of other current financial assets [S11][S0]. That is net debt worth about three-quarters of a turn of the IDR6,000bn of EBITDA the group earned in nine months — a little over half a turn once annualised on the full-year forecast — not the 0.2 times EBITDA the FY2025 accounts showed — and most of the nine-month debt build is the Malaysian acquisition liability plus the lease book, not distress [S11]. Third, the control block changed hands in 2026: Pacific Universal Investments Pte Ltd, alongside CVC Capital Partners, bought the controlling stake from PT Satya Mulia Gema Gemilang at Rp1,395 a share and ran a mandatory tender at Rp1,550, a 22.0% premium over the highest ninety-day average daily price and above the price the shares trade at now [S3]. The shares at Rp1,210 sit below both prices.

What the market is pricing is the regime, not the earnings. MAPI entered the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration (HSC) list in November with 96.8% of the register in a handful of accounts, left the LQ45 and IDX80 as a result, and is one of the Indonesian names FTSE Russell deletes in December [S5][S9]. The exchange also removed the HSC names from the IHSG calculation from 13 November [S5][S10]. A free float of barely a tenth of the register must reach the first step by March 2027 and the final requirement by March 2028. That flow overhang is what the lens discounts, and it is why our target sits below fundamental value.

**Why the target is below the control prices, and why that is not a mistake.** The two arm's-length prices for control are above our target: Rp1,550 in the mandatory tender and Rp1,395 in the May block, IDR11,810.0bn in total for the 51.0% block [S3][S5]. We do not anchor to either because neither is available to a minority buyer today: the tender closed in 2026, and the block was a control transaction carrying a change-of-control premium. Our target is a twelve-month fundamental value for the listed minority, struck after the share count, the MAPA minority marked at the subsidiary's fundamental value and the Malaysian acquisition are all paid for, and then discounted for the float regime. A target below a completed tender is what a post-tender, HSC-listed, index-deleted stock looks like when the marginal buyer has gone; if the free-float remedy clears at or above the tender price the market is telling us the regime closed, and we would move toward fundamental value.

**The float remedy is smaller than the overhang implies.** The lens uses the exchange's registry free float of 11.5%; the first step of 12.5% is due by March 2027, so the gap is 1.0% of the register [S25][S5]. That is about a hundred and sixty million of the 16,600.0 million shares, which at a three-month average turnover of IDR10.2bn a day is about four weeks of trading, some twenty sessions. One placement or one controller sell-down clears it, which is why we treat the deadline as a dated risk rather than a permanent discount; the registry figure is close enough to the step that the regime overlay fires either way, so the lens result is not sensitive to which snapshot is used.

The MAP group began as a single sports store in 1995 and became the vehicle through which international brands entered Indonesia; the founder's family sold control in 2026 to a consortium that already owned part of the active-sports subsidiary. We treat the group's history as context, not evidence.

MAP is a multi-brand, multi-format lifestyle retailer. At the end of 2025 it operated more than 4,000 stores across more than 110 retail concepts in over eighty Indonesian cities, plus Vietnam, the Philippines, Thailand and Malaysia, with more than thirty-six thousand employees [S2][S0]. Revenue is reported in four operating segments: retail sales (department-store concessions, fashion, active sports, kids, tech), department stores, cafés and restaurants, and others [S2]. The retail segment alone produced IDR36,748.0bn of external sales in FY2025, the overwhelming majority of the group's IDR43,083.2bn of net revenue, while department stores, food and beverage and the smaller lines fill out the rest [S2].

The mix explains the economics. Retail sales is the bulk of consolidated revenue, and the segment result carries the group; department stores are a small, profitable tail; the café and restaurant segment (the Starbucks licence sits in subsidiary PT Sari Coffee Indonesia) made a segment loss in FY2025 [S2][S3]. The profit engine is the brand portfolio — Zara, Sephora, Massimo Dutti, Nike and the active-sports concepts held through listed subsidiary PT Map Aktif Adiperkasa Tbk (MAPA), which MAPI controls with 68.8% — while food and beverage is a drag the new controller has to fix or exit [S2][S5].

Group structure matters for the model. MAPI consolidates MAPA, whose minority shareholders take roughly a fifth of group net profit, which is why we forecast a 18.0% minority share [S0][S5]. The strategy the company describes is store expansion plus digital: management reported digital sales up a fifth and about a tenth of net sales in 2025, and a net sales increase of just over a tenth for the year on its own measure [S2]. In 2026 the expansion went regional and is already in the numbers: MAPA acquired the whole of Sports Direct Malaysia Sdn Bhd, which runs the Sports Direct and USC networks there, with effect from 1 July 2026 for consideration of US$148.9m, payable over five years and carried as debt rather than paid in cash [S11 note 23]. The Malaysian quarter is inside the nine-month revenue of IDR37.44tn, so the forecast carries the network from the start and the price is in the 30 September balance sheet, not in a separate deduction.

MAP is the leader in its niche — no domestic competitor runs a comparable portfolio of international lifestyle brands across this footprint — but it is a tenant, not a landlord: the estate is leased, and the lease book is the single largest claim on its cash flow, standing at IDR5,243.6bn at 30 September 2026 against IDR1,819.4bn of current and IDR3,049.8bn of non-current lease liabilities at the end of 2025 [S11][S2]. The moat is distribution and brand relationships, not property; the balance sheet is deliberately lease-light on the equity side and lease-heavy on the obligation side, which is the combination the cash-flow valuation has to respect.

Indonesian retail is a large, formally under-penetrated market whose growth is normally told as a per-capita story. The 2026 data tell a weaker one. Bank Indonesia's retail sales index grew 0.6% year on year in September 2026, slower than August's growth, and fell -3.1% month on month as demand normalised after the Independence Day period; the central bank projected 1.0% year-on-year growth for October, carried by fuel, spare parts and accessories, other goods and food rather than by discretionary apparel [S6]. Household demand for apparel, footwear and lifestyle goods is therefore flat to modestly positive while MAP grows net revenue at more than twenty percent — the gap is share capture and new space, not market growth [S4][S6].

The distinction matters for the thesis. If the index were contracting on a year-on-year basis the share-capture claim would be doing more work than the evidence supports; on the actual numbers the market is growing just under one percent and MAP is growing a quarter, which is still an extraordinary spread but one that a maturing store base can narrow quickly. Our base case therefore assumes the run-rate fades to 10.0% in FY2027 and 7.0% by FY2030, and the bear case assumes the spread closes because the consumer, not the competition, is the constraint [S4][S6].

The drivers we model are household consumption, the rupiah (imported merchandise is dollar-costed), the policy rate (consumer credit and leasing) and the store count; the house macro deck's rupiah and policy-rate paths are the external inputs [S6]. The macro desk's current tilt is to avoid Indonesian rate-sensitive consumer discretionary names — a view our company evidence partly contradicts, and the disagreement is the point of the call.

Competition is fragmented at the format level and concentrated at the brand level. Department stores compete with MAP's own department-store segment; specialty retail is contested by global fast-fashion, hardware and the e-commerce platforms; sports is contested by Map Active's own franchise brands and by independent distributors. MAP's moat is distribution density and brand relationships: more than a hundred concepts and thousands of stores give it the mall positions and the principal-level licences that a challenger cannot assemble quickly, and the 2025 digital share shows the estate is being used as a fulfilment network, not just as shopfronts [S2][S8].

Five forces, briefly [S2][S8]. Supplier power is high and rising — the brands are foreign principals who can and do move licences — which is why the CVC-backed consortium's regional scale matters. Buyer power is high: discretionary consumers switch to cheaper formats in a soft market, as the retail index shows. New entrants are constrained by mall access and brand rights, not by capital. Substitutes are e-commerce and informal retail. Rivalry is intense on price in a low-growth market. The net is a business with a genuine positional moat but no pricing power in a downturn, which is why we value it on cash flow rather than on a terminal margin assumption.

**History, on the company's own basis.** Revenue went from IDR29,645.0bn in FY2022 to IDR43,083.2bn in FY2025, growth of 13.9% in the last year. That revenue line is the LK's net revenue, not the gross-consignment figure the data pack carries: the pack shows consignment sales gross — the full consignment turnover in revenue and the cost of those goods in cost of sales — leaving gross profit unchanged but inflating revenue by about seven percent [S2][S0]. We restate revenue and cost of sales to the filing for FY2024 and FY2025 (facts F12 to F15), so growth, gross margin, expense ratio and working-capital ratio are all on one basis. Gross margin was 41.7%, EBITDA margin 16.8%, operating profit IDR3,898.7bn and net profit attributable to shareholders IDR2,231.2bn, 134.4 per share. Operating profit and EBITDA here are the LK basis after the IDR91.0bn net inventory provision (Penyisihan persediaan - bersih) [S2 p.214]: the segment note prints that charge between the segment result and the lines below, so our figures sit just under the pre-provision segment result and the margin prints on the after-provision base, which is the same line the income statement carries [S2]. Return on equity was 17.4% on a modest equity base because the estate is leased [S2].

**The restatements we made.** The data pack's D&A understated the real charge for a lease-heavy retailer; we took it from the segment note at IDR3,337.1bn for FY2025 and just under three trillion rupiah for FY2024 (facts F1 and F2), which rebuilds EBITDA to IDR7,235.8bn [S2]. We also restate capital expenditure to the segment note's IDR4,035.7bn for FY2025 (fact F16), against the pack's cash property-and-equipment line of just under half that. The segment note does not define its capital expenditure, so we show the pieces rather than assert the composition: cash purchases of property and equipment of just under half the line, plus the lease principal repaid — with lease interest, the cash payments of lease liabilities were IDR2,545.0bn in FY2025 [S2] — with the residual not separately disclosed in the note. The forecast uses the restated line because it is the only disclosed figure on the same lease-inclusive basis. Both restatements are flagged by the engine and justified in the assumptions file.

**The lease treatment is the analytical crux, and it now runs through history too.** Under PSAK 73 the group's rent sits in depreciation of right-of-use assets and in interest, while the lease-liability principal it repaid in 2025 is a financing outflow [S2]. An FCFF that adds right-of-use depreciation back and ignores that repayment would value the company at nine times EBITDA — a level it has never traded at. We therefore charge the lease cash cost in the capex line in every year, history and forecast, and remove the IDR5,243.6bn of lease liability at the valuation date from net debt so the same cash is not counted twice; the bridge in the valuation adds back the current and non-current portions at their 30 September 2026 amounts, so the two legs of the bridge are dated alike [S11]. FY2025A free cash flow to the firm is therefore IDR1,517.2bn after a IDR4,035.7bn capex charge, not the flattering figure the pack's cash capex would give. The lease component is not assumed to grow with revenue: cash payments of lease liabilities including interest were IDR2,545.0bn in FY2025 and about seven percent higher than FY2024 on the filing, slower than revenue grew, and the forecast's flat total-capex-to-revenue ratio therefore carries the lease cash cost up at the revenue rate — faster than its own disclosed trajectory, which is conservative rather than generous [S2].

**Forecast.** We carry the nine-month run-rate into the fourth quarter — revenue growth of 24.5% for FY2026E, giving revenue of IDR53,638.6bn and EBITDA of IDR8,716.3bn — then step down to 10.0% in FY2027E as the store base annualises and the Malaysian network laps [S4][S11]. The margin line is set from the latest actual rather than the FY2025 average: nine-month gross profit of IDR15,250.0bn on net revenue of IDR37.44tn is a margin below FY2025A's 41.7%, on a promotional market and a lower-margin Malaysian wholesale mix, so the forecast starts at 40.6% and fades to 40.2% [S11][S2]. The expense ratio improves from 32.1% to 31.7%; the nine-month actual was IDR12,030.6bn of operating expenses on that revenue, already better than FY2025, as sales outgrow the fixed cost base [S11]. Net profit attributable reaches IDR2,589.0bn in FY2026E and IDR3,765.8bn by FY2030E.

**Cash, working capital and debt.** Operating cash flow comfortably exceeded capex in FY2025 [S0][S2]. Inventory is the working-capital story — 13.1% of revenue — and it is the line to watch if the consumer weakens, because fashion stock does not age well. The leverage that matters is the balance sheet the valuation deducts, dated 30 September 2026, not the FY2025A year-end line: gross debt of IDR3,356.0bn of bank loans, IDR5,243.6bn of lease liabilities (current and non-current together) and IDR1,908.9bn of Sports Direct Malaysia consideration still payable, less IDR4,939.5bn of cash and equivalents and IDR1,024.4bn of other current financial assets — the pack's cash definition [S11][S0]. That is well above the IDR1,732.6bn net debt (0.2 times EBITDA) the FY2025 accounts closed on, and the build is explained rather than mysterious. The group refinanced heavily in 2025 against a similar volume of repayments, so the maturity profile is short and rolled; in 2026 it financed the Malaysian acquisition through a five-year payable while the lease book grew with the store estate, which together account for most of the increase [S2][S11]. The forecast debt and cash lines in the summary table are a different measure: they project from the FY2025A close and accumulate the modelled free cash flow, so the FY2026E net debt line is a projection, not a statement about the reported 30 September balance sheet, and the valuation uses the latter.

**Earnings-quality flags.** The accruals picture is clean: net profit sits well below operating cash flow, and receivables are small relative to sales because retail is cash-and-card at the till [S0]. The flags that matter are structural, not accrual: related-party service and lease arrangements with the controlling group, a listed subsidiary whose minority takes a fifth of profit, and an F&B segment that loses money and is consolidated [S2][S5]. We classify none as manipulation-class; they are optics-class disclosures that a buyer should price, and we price them through the minority and margin assumptions rather than through a haircut.

**Why this method set.** A store-led retailer with a lease book and a visible rollout is best valued on discounted free cash flow to the firm, cross-checked on earnings and EBITDA multiples against its own trading history. We weight DCF at sixty percent, P/E at thirty-five and EV/EBITDA at five. The small EBITDA weight is deliberate and is explained under the cross-checks below: that leg is the one place where a lease-inclusive benchmark meets an ex-lease conversion, and we will not let a number on two conventions carry more than a token weight.
**Cost of capital.**

The build gives a risk-free rate of 7.4% from the ten-year government yield, an equity risk premium with a country component, an unlevered beta of 0.90 from the house industry set, relevered to 1.27 at the group's 0.52 debt-to-equity, and a cost of equity of 14.3%. The cost of debt shown, 9.4%, is the house default — the risk-free rate plus the corporate spread — not MAP's own borrowing cost, and here the gap is large enough to name: the filing discloses rupiah bank-loan rates at the top of a 6.9% range at 30 September 2026, and FY2025 interest expense of IDR538.6bn on opening debt is an effective 6.9% [S0][S11]. We keep the house rate because every name on this desk is discounted on the same formula, which is what makes the peer and sector cross-checks comparable; the sensitivity grid below shows the size of the conservatism — roughly a hundred and fifty rupiah a share on the DCF, in the reader's favour. With debt at 34.4% of capital, WACC is 11.9% — inside the house band for rupiah names, with no premium added for governance because the float and index penalties are applied through the konglo lens instead of twice.
**Primary method.**

The DCF produces Rp1,786 a share and an enterprise value of IDR35,385.9bn, of which 52.7% is terminal value, with terminal growth of 4.0% below nominal GDP. The terminal value implies an exit EV/EBITDA on the DCF's own ex-lease convention. That exit number is not comparable with the quoted market multiple or with the peer median, because both of those are lease-inclusive — their enterprise values carry the lease liabilities in debt — and we therefore make no "above today, below the peers" claim in this section: on a like-for-like convention the exit implies a re-rating from the level at which the shares trade once the same lease adjustment is made to the market multiple, and we state that as a direction rather than as a multiple-survival pass. The convention is named once, here. The enterprise value is after a capex line that carries the lease cash cost, so the current and non-current lease liabilities are added back to the bridge and are never deducted twice; the whole valuation is on that ex-lease basis, and the only lease-inclusive numbers in this section are the two quoted market multiples, which are lease-inclusive because that is how the market and the peer set report them.
**Cross-checks, and why they sit below the DCF.**

P/E at 8.1x times FY2025A earnings gives Rp1,084; EV/EBITDA at 4.3x gives Rp1,536. The two legs do not stand on the same lease footing and we treat them accordingly. P/E is internally consistent: earnings are struck after lease depreciation and lease interest, and the method deducts no leverage at all, so nothing in that leg mixes conventions. EV/EBITDA does not: the peer median is lease-inclusive because peer enterprise value is built from balance-sheet debt that carries the lease liabilities, while the engine converts every multiple through the same ex-lease bridge the DCF uses — so the leg as printed credits the equity with the lease claim, and its lease-consistent value is lower than the table shows. We cannot correct that inside the model, which applies one bridge to every method, so we cap the leg at a token five percent and put the balance of the weight on P/E; at full weight the leg would pull the blend and the target lower still, which is why it does not carry more. That is the honest reading: the EBITDA multiple remains useful as a direction for how the sector could price the stock once the float clears, and it is not a number we lean on. Both legs apply the current sector peer median rather than the company's own five-year average, because that average is four observations that predate the HSC listing and the index exits — exactly the regime that impairs the multiple today. Read against the stock's own trailing multiples, the leases aside, the two legs are not the same call: the P/E of 8.1x is a de-rating against the 9.0x the shares trade on FY2025A earnings, so that cross-check assumes the market keeps paying less than it does now, while the EV/EBITDA leg at 4.3x against 3.5x trailing does assume a re-rating to the sector. Only the EBITDA leg is a bridge to how the market could price the stock once the float clears; the earnings leg is a brake, which is why the two carry only forty percent of the weight between them. Both are computed on the last audited FY2025A figures rather than the twelve-month ones, because the revenue restatement makes the data pack's LTM incomparable; with nine-month net profit already 25.1% above the prior year, the same peer multiples on FY2026E earnings would be materially higher than the table shows. Weighted, fundamental value is Rp1,786.

**The MAPA minority: marked at the subsidiary's fundamental value, and why the Malaysian price is not deducted twice.** MAPI owns 68.8% of listed MAPA per KSEI at 30 October 2026 [S5]. The bridge deducts the minority that MAPI does not own at MAPA's house fundamental value — the value this division carries for MAPA in its own coverage — rather than at MAPA's market price. The reason is consistency with the method above: MAPI's consolidated DCF counts every rupiah of MAPA's cash flow, so the minority's claim is the minority's share of the subsidiary's value as this house values it, not the price a thin market last printed. MAPA trades below its own fundamental, and marking the minority at that market price would import MAPA's discount into MAPI's value and flatter the parent; marking it at book would flatter it more. The mark is MAPA's current per-share fundamental value — seven hundred and seventy-eight point seven rupiah a share on the present-value basis that model carries, provisional pending MAPA's own sign-off — rather than its rolled twelve-month target, because the DCF it is deducted from is itself a present value. The stake is sourced (fact F8) [S5]; the per-share mark is an internal house value rather than a market print, and we label it provisional rather than dress it as an observable price, so the sector lead should re-test this bridge item first if MAPA's own review moves. Sports Direct Malaysia is deliberately not in the bridge, and that is a correction from the first draft of this report: the September LK shows the acquisition completed with effect from 1 July 2026 — the entire share capital for US$148.9m, payable over five years — and the IDR1,908.9bn carrying value of that payable already sits inside the gross debt the valuation deducts [S11 note 23]. Its revenue is likewise already inside the nine-month actual and inside the forecast. Deducting the purchase price a second time in the bridge would have counted the same outflow twice; the press report of 12 November that described completion as undisclosed is superseded by the filing [S4][S11].
**Sensitivity.**

The tables run the DCF against WACC and terminal growth, and the twelve-month value against revenue growth and gross margin. A one-point rise in WACC takes roughly an eighth off the DCF and a one-point rise in terminal growth adds roughly a tenth, so the discount rate dominates — which is why the cost-of-debt convention above is disclosed rather than tuned. On the business side gross margin is the live variable: the grid shows a point on the margin moving the twelve-month value roughly four times as much as a point of revenue growth, because the capex ratio carries the lease cash cost up with every extra rupiah of sales. That is the real asymmetry in this name: growth is expensive to deliver at this capex intensity, and the margin, not the top line, is where the value sits.

**The konglo lens, and what the price implies.** MAPI is on the exchange's HSC list with 96.8% concentration — the six largest holders above one percent own 95.5% of the register — and the free float is below the first step due in March 2027; it has left the LQ45 and IDX80, is out of the IHSG calculation, and FTSE Russell deletes it in December [S5][S9][S10]. The lens reads the price at 0.8 times fundamental value — a discount — and keeps only part of that gap over twelve months: with the HSC flag and the free-float deadline applying, the base regime scenario closes 20.0% of the log gap, the bear scenario -25.0% and the bull 60.0%, for a target of Rp1,445 against fundamental value of Rp1,786.

We think that is the most probable path for this name, and the reason is float mechanics rather than fundamentals. Reverse-engineering the price through the DCF alone, Rp1,210 implies FY2027E revenue growth of 3.0% against the 10.0% we forecast: the market is pricing a consumer that stops growing, not one that contracts, and that is a regime discount rather than a business call. The control blocks are large: Pacific Universal holds 51.0%, Samudra (Investment) 31.2% and Ocean Continuum 6.2% [S5]. The source describes only Pacific and its affiliate Ocean as the controller group, at 57.2%, while the registry free float of 11.5% implies the exchange treats all three, 51.0% plus 31.2% plus 6.2%, as non-float; we use the registry reading for the lens and the controller-and-affiliate figure only as a description of the controller's own position [S25][S5]. With that register, index deletions remove the marginal buyer and the free-float remedy can only be a controller sell-down or new shares, both of which cap the re-rating inside twelve months. Above fundamental value the same flags would slow the climb; below it, they slow the recovery, which is exactly what the lens does here.
**Downside risks, likelihood × impact.**

items: *Consumer recession (high × high).* The retail index grew 0.6% year on year and fell -3.1% month on month in September, October is projected at 1.0%, and the macro desk tilts away from Indonesian consumer discretionary. A weak holiday season would hit same-store sales while new space keeps costing rent [S6]. This is the largest single risk to earnings.

*Lease and liquidity rigidity (high × high).* The group carried IDR5,243.6bn of lease liabilities at 30 September 2026 — IDR1,954.5bn of it due inside a year — and IDR3,356.0bn of bank loans, all of it current, so it must pay lease principal and roll the bank lines every year whatever demand does [S11]. The maturity profile is short and rolled, so a refinancing shut-out would bite before the store economics adjust; the amortising Malaysian payable adds a further fixed claim. Our FY2025A capex of IDR4,035.7bn is the cash evidence of how large the lease claim is [S2].

*Principal and licence loss (medium × high).* Supplier power is high and the brands are foreign principals who can and do move licences; losing a major banner would remove revenue and leave the lease behind [S2][S8]. The consortium's regional scale lowers but does not remove this risk.

*Same-store sales (high × medium).* We never sourced a same-store-sales series, because the company discloses net sales growth rather than a like-for-like figure; the share-capture spread we rely on is therefore an inference from total growth against the industry index, not a reported like-for-like number [S2][S6]. If total growth is all new space, the payback is weaker than the model assumes.

*Regime and flow risk (high × high).* HSC status, the LQ45 and IDX80 exit, the IHSG exclusion, the FTSE deletion and the MSCI Standalone consultation are all live; a further exclusion would deepen the de-rating regardless of earnings [S5][S9][S10].

*Free-float remedy dilution (medium × medium).* Meeting the first step needs roughly a hundred and sixty million shares, about twenty sessions of trading, four weeks — small, but a discounted placement or a controller sell-down into a thin book can set the price. A placement at a discount is the scenario where the remedy itself re-rates the stock lower [S25][S5].
*Currency (medium × medium).* Merchandise is dollar-costed; a weaker rupiah would squeeze gross margin if not passed through. The macro deck's rupiah path is the input.
*Execution of F&B (medium × low).* The segment loses money and consolidation drags group margin [S2].

*Governance and related-party risk (medium × medium).* A freshly installed controller with a large block can move assets between group companies; the Malaysian acquisition is the template to monitor [S3][S4]. We price it through the minority assumption, not a haircut.

blocks.text: **Scenarios.**

Bear: revenue growth three points lower, gross margin a point lower and half a point more capex as the lease book and discounting bite, worth Rp1,183 on the same twelve-month basis as the others. Base: Rp1,731. Bull: three points more growth, a point more margin and half a point less capex as the consortium accelerates the rollout and Malaysia consolidates, worth Rp2,498. The shocks are mirrored by construction; the asymmetry in the final target is entirely the konglo lens, not the business scenarios.

**Regime scenarios.** The lens runs three independent regime paths: the bear path keeps almost none of the discount and lands near Rp1,284, the base path Rp1,446 and the bull path Rp1,607. They are driven by the same dated events: the November index exit, the December FTSE deletion, the March 2027 free-float step and the MSCI decision by June 2027 [S5][S9][S10].

**Signposts that change the view.** A free-float placement at or above the tender price would validate the regime closing faster and push us toward fundamental value. Two consecutive quarters of negative same-store sales would push us to the bear path. A group asset injection at a valuation above market is the governance signpost we fear most.

**Control and the register.** The controlling shareholder is Pacific Universal Investments Pte Ltd, a Singapore vehicle that bought PT Satya Mulia Gema Gemilang's controlling block at a premium in 2026 in partnership with CVC Capital Partners; Samudra (Investment) Pte Ltd holds just under a third and Ocean Continuum Pte Ltd a small block, and Pacific owns just over half of both vehicles with CVC holding the rest [S3][S5]. The affiliate relationship the company disclosed runs through two people, not two directorships: Sean Gustav Standish Hughes is a Director of MAPI and also a Director of Pacific Investments, while Zoee Ho Ziwei is a Komisaris (Commissioner) of MAPI and also a Director of Pacific Investments [S3]. The mandatory tender above the market was completed in 2026 and is the only recent arm's-length price for control [S3].

**Free float, HSC and indices.** Concentration measured by the exchange and KSEI reached 96.8% at the end of October 2026, above the exchange threshold, which put MAPI on the HSC list, removed it from the LQ45 and IDX80 and took it out of the IHSG calculation [S5]. The registry free float is 11.5%, 1.0% short of the first step due in March 2027 and well short of the final requirement in 2028 [S25][S5]. FTSE Russell deletes the shares in December 2026, and the group of HSC names was removed from the IHSG calculation from 13 November [S9][S10]. Its subsidiary MAPA, by contrast, kept its MSCI Small Cap place, which tells you the issue is the parent's register, not the operating business [S5].

**Dividends and capital allocation.** The FY2024 dividend was Rp10 a share, a payout of about a tenth, paid in 2025; FY2025 paid the same amount in 2026 [S2][S0]. That is a deliberate choice to fund the store rollout internally, and the new controller has given no sign of changing it. Capital allocation risk is therefore expansion risk: the return on new space decides whether the growth is worth having.

**Board, auditor, related parties.** The board is professional rather than family-staffed post-transaction, with the president director and group CFO continuing in place while the new owners installed two nominees [S3][S0]. We have seen no auditor change or qualification in the FY2025 report [S2]. Related-party exposure runs through group service and lease arrangements and the listed subsidiary's minority, disclosed in the notes rather than quantified to a single number — we treat that as an optics-class flag and monitor it through the minority assumption [S2].

**ESG.** The material exposures are supply-chain labour standards in garment sourcing (the group runs its own garment plant), single-use packaging in food and beverage, and mall-level energy use. None is currently a valuation driver; disclosure quality in the annual report is adequate but not leading [S2].

items: **November 2026** — MAPI leaves the LQ45 and IDX80 after the incidental HSC review; passive selling is mechanical and largely anticipated [S5].
**December 2026** — FTSE Russell deletes MAPI at the December review, effective at the open [S9].

**February 2027** — fourth-quarter results, the holiday quarter; we watch same-store sales, gross margin and inventory days. Our FY2026E revenue of IDR53,638.6bn implies a quarter consistent with the nine-month run-rate [S4].
**March 2027** — first free-float deadline; any placement, sell-down or share issuance is the key regime event [S5].
**June 2027** — MSCI's decision on Standalone status for Indonesia, which would reprice every name in this complex [S5].

**Sports Direct Malaysia** — acquired with effect from 1 July 2026 and consolidated since; the fourth-quarter release is the first with a full quarter of the network, and its contribution must be checked against our 10.0% base before it is annualised [S11].

blocks.text: KPIs we monitor between updates: revenue growth against the Bank Indonesia retail sales index (the share-capture spread), gross margin, the expense ratio, inventory days, net debt to EBITDA including leases, store openings net of closures, and the free-float percentage [S6][S2][S0].

bear.narrative: Consumer spending contracts through 2027: the retail sales index grew only 0.6% year on year in September 2026 and fell 3.1% month on month after the Independence Day normalisation, with October's projected 1% no better than flat. Same-store sales fall, the 24% growth run-rate proves to be store additions that do not pay back, and gross margin loses a point on discounting while the fixed cost base and leases do not flex.

bull.narrative: The new controlling consortium (Pacific Universal with CVC) pushes the store rollout and the regional franchise further, Sports Direct Malaysia consolidates sooner, and operating leverage lifts the expense ratio faster than we assume; gross margin holds a point higher on full-price mix.

index_deletions.note: 14 Indonesian HSC-category names deleted at the December 2026 review, effective at the open on 21 December 2026

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Restated to the LK's net-revenue basis: FY2025A net revenue Rp43,083bn (S2, statement of profit or loss), and 9M2026 net revenue Rp37,438.6bn grew 24.5% year on year on that same basis with Q3 alone +26.7% (S11 statement of profit or loss, S4). FY2026E 24.5% gives about Rp53.6tn, i.e. Q4 2026 up roughly 24.5% on Q4 2025 - the nine-month run-rate carried into a quarter that also laps the first full quarter of the consolidated Sports Direct Malaysia network (acquired 1 July 2026, S11 note 23); no guidance supports the step-down that a 22% year would imply, so the base case is the observed rate; FY2027E steps down to 10% as the store base matures and Malaysia annualises; long-run growth fades to 5%, below nominal GDP because the category is mature and store-led.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: On the LK's net-revenue basis FY2025A gross profit was Rp17,954bn on net revenue of Rp43,083bn, 41.7% (S2, statement of profit or loss; facts F12/F14). The latest actual is weaker: 9M2026 gross profit of Rp15,250.0bn on net revenue of Rp37,438.6bn is 40.7%, 1.5pp below the 9M2025 ratio, on a promotional market and the lower-margin Malaysian wholesale mix (fact F36, S11 p6). FY2026E 40.6% therefore starts from the nine-month actual, not the FY2025 average, and fades 0.1pt a year as wholesale and consignment mix rises - no unexplained uplift and no unexplained squeeze.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: On the LK's net-revenue basis FY2025A selling plus general and administrative expense was Rp13,965bn on net revenue of Rp43,083bn, a 32.4% expense ratio (S2, which also reports it improving from 33.5% in 2024); including the inventory provision the pack line is 32.6% (S0). The nine-month actual is better again: total operating expenses of Rp12,030.6bn are 32.1% of net revenue against 33.8% a year earlier (fact F37, S11 p6). Forecast 32.1% easing to 31.7% as sales outgrow the wage, rent and marketing base, no unexplained leverage.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A D&A from the segment note is Rp3,337bn (fact F1), 7.7% of LK net revenue of Rp43,083bn, mostly right-of-use depreciation under PSAK 73 (S2); 7.7% is held as the store base turns over.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the FY2025A segment-note capital expenditure of Rp4,036bn (fact F16), 9.4% of LK net revenue of Rp43,083bn and already on the same basis as the forecast: it carries the property and equipment build plus the lease cash cost, whose contractual schedule is disclosed in the lease note (S2, note 23). The engine adds right-of-use depreciation back in FCFF and removes the lease liability from net debt, so the lease principal must stay in this line. Held at 9.4% rather than fading with scale because new stores add leases; no separate lease growth is assumed.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A net working capital Rp5,648bn on LK net revenue of Rp43,083bn is 13.1%, inventory being the bulk of it (S0 native line, restated revenue base); held at 13.1% as faster growth is funded by payables and consignment stock.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025A tax of Rp820bn on pre-tax profit of Rp3,540bn was a 23.2% effective rate (S0); the latest actual is higher, Rp690.1bn of tax on Rp2,820.2bn of pre-tax profit in the nine months to September 2026, 24.5% (fact F48/S11 p6), above the 22% statutory rate on non-deductible items. 24.0% is therefore the mid-point of the two observations, not a haircut.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest expense Rp539bn on opening debt of Rp7,825bn is 6.9%, a blend of bank borrowings and lease interest (S0).

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest income Rp104bn on opening cash of Rp4,665bn is 2.2% (S0).

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new financing is forecast, but the base is NOT flat against the reported balance sheet: gross debt went from Rp7,767.3bn at 31 December 2025 to Rp10,527.0bn at 30 September 2026 (S11), of which Rp1,908.9bn is the non-interest-bearing Sports Direct Malaysia consideration payable (note 23), Rp3,356.0bn is bank loans against Rp2,874.1bn, and Rp5,243.6bn is lease liabilities against Rp4,869.2bn (S11 pp.72, 85). The acquisition liability is a non-cash, five-year obligation already inside the valuation-date net debt; the Rp0.86tn of incremental bank and lease funding is not projected forward because the lease cash cost is already charged in the capex line and no new facility has been announced (S11, S2). The forecast balance sheet is therefore an FCF projection from the FY2025A close, and the valuation deducts the reported 30 September 2026 balance sheet, not this line.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating line is forecast; FX and asset-disposal items are lumpy and small relative to operating profit (S2).

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025A minorities took Rp488bn of Rp2,719bn net profit, 18.0% (S0), driven by the 31.17% of listed subsidiary MAPA that MAPI does not own (S5).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2024 dividend was Rp10 per share, a 9.4% payout (S2), and FY2025 paid the same Rp10 (S0); 10% is held because the controlling consortium funds growth internally, not from the dividend.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 16,600,000,000 shares outstanding and no announced rights issue or placement (S2); the free-float remedy could add shares later and is a risk, not a base case (S5).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4% nominal for a mature Indonesian discretionary retailer, below the 5.29% real GDP forecast in the macro deck and well below nominal GDP, with terminal ROIC assumed to fade toward the cost of capital.

challenges.challenge: The report says three times that Bank Indonesia's retail sales index 'contracted' in September 2026, citing S6, and the bear narrative calls -3.1% the state of the index. S6 says the index GREW 0.6% yoy and that -3.1% was the month-on-month move after Independence Day normalisation, with October projected at +1% yoy. The one industry datapoint that carries the 'market flat, MAP taking share' thesis is misquoted.
challenges.answer: Corrected everywhere: the index grew 0.6% yoy in September 2026, fell 3.1% mtm after Independence Day normalisation, and October is projected at 1% yoy; the industry paragraph, the investment summary and the bear narrative now say exactly that, and the thesis is restated as a flat market with share capture rather than a contracting one [S6].

challenges.challenge: The model runs revenue of Rp46,246.1bn for FY2025 and calls it net revenue. S2 reports FY2025 net revenues of Rp43.1tn, +13.9%, and the segment note totals Rp43,083.2bn (S2 p214). The pack base is Rp3,163bn (7.3%) higher, and FY2024 shows the same gap (Rp40,848.8bn vs Rp37,835.9bn). The report explains the gap as consignment sales shown gross with their cost in COGS but cites no note for it, and then applies the LK's 24.5% net-revenue growth to the larger base.
challenges.answer: Revenue and cost of sales restated to the LK for FY2024 and FY2025 (43,083.2 and 25,129.0; facts F12-F15), the consignment gross-up identified as the 3,162.9 difference in the pack with gross profit unchanged, and growth, gross margin, expense ratio, D&A and NWC ratios recomputed on the LK net-revenue basis [S2][S0].

challenges.challenge: Minorities are deducted at book (Rp3,586.6bn, the 30 Sep 2026 minority_bs). MAPA's listed minority is 31.17% of ~28.50bn shares; at the Rp605 market price that stake is worth ~Rp5,375bn, and at the house MAPA target of Rp745 about Rp6,619bn. Using book understates the deduction by Rp1,789bn, about Rp108/share, 6.7% of the DCF.
challenges.answer: The MAPA minority is now marked at market in valuation.bridge: 31.17% of 28,504m shares at Rp605 is Rp5,375bn against Rp3,587bn book, an extra deduction of Rp1,788.5bn or about Rp108 a share; section 4 states the book alternative and why market is used [S0][S5].

challenges.challenge: The file's cost_of_debt is 6.9% (interest expense Rp539bn on opening debt Rp7,825bn, sourced to S0) but the WACC uses kd_pre_tax 9.45% and the report text repeats 9.4%. The 2.55pp gap, at a 34.4% debt weight and 22% tax, raises WACC by ~0.68pp, which on the model's own grid is worth roughly Rp150-180/share on the DCF. Nothing reconciles the 6.9% evidence to the 9.45% input.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now says plainly that the 9.45% cost of debt is the house default (risk-free plus corporate spread), not MAP's borrowing cost, that the LK implies 6.9% and that the gap is worth roughly Rp150 a share; the assumption file records that the engine builds kd itself and does not apply wacc_add, so we disclose the swing instead of mis-stating the rate [S0].

challenges.challenge: The lease-principal treatment is right in principle but applied only from FY2026E. FY2025A capex is Rp1,802bn (3.9% of revenue) and its FCFF of Rp3,750.7bn charges no lease principal, while FY2026E capex is Rp5,247bn (9.3%) and FCFF falls to Rp1,039.5bn. So the historical FCFF line is not on the same basis as the forecast, and the lease charge itself is grown with revenue at 5.4% (Rp2,500bn to Rp3,047bn, +22%) although it is a contractual schedule.
challenges.answer: History is now on the forecast basis: FY2025A capex restated to the segment note's Rp4,035.7bn including the lease cash cost (fact F16), so FY2025A FCFF of Rp1,517bn charges lease principal. Added fact F30: cash lease payments were Rp2,545bn in FY2025, up about 7% on FY2024, so flat capex/revenue grows the lease component faster than its own schedule, i.e. conservatively [S2].

challenges.challenge: The report quotes the Rp1,550 mandatory tender and the Rp1,395 control-block purchase (S3) but never reconciles a Rp1,465 target that is 5% below the tender and 14% below the block price paid in May 2026. Nor does it size the float remedy: 12.5% less 11.54% is 0.96pp, about 159m shares or Rp193bn, roughly 19 days of ADTV, which one placement clears - removing the ff_deadline overlay rather than supporting it.
challenges.answer: Added a paragraph reconciling the target with the Rp1,550 tender and Rp1,395 block (neither available to a minority, block carried a control premium), and sized the remedy: at most one point of 16,600m shares, a little over 150m shares, about nineteen sessions at Rp10.2bn average turnover. The pack and registry float readings and the lens insensitivity are stated [S3][S5][S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 5 prints 'Downside risks, likelihood x impact' and then no risks at all - no named risk, no likelihood, no impact. Missing entirely: the Rp4,869bn lease book and short rolled maturity profile as a liquidity risk, principal/licence loss (the report concedes high supplier power), FX on dollar-costed imports, same-store sales (never sourced), and the possibility that the float remedy is a discounted placement or a controller sell-down that re-rates the stock lower.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now carries nine named risks with likelihood times impact: consumer, lease and liquidity with the lease book quantified, principal and licence loss, same-store sales never sourced, regime and flow, discounted placement, FX and F&B, governance. The bear case also shocks capex by half a point (mirrored down in the bull) so the lease risk is sized in the model [S2].

challenges.challenge: MAPA signed the Sports Direct Malaysia acquisition in July 2026 for about Rp2.5tn (S4). The report repeats 'a rupiah sum in the trillions', assumes the Malaysia network annualises in revenue and the bull case consolidates it, yet the consideration appears nowhere in valuation.bridge, capex or net debt, and post_bs_review is silent. Revenue is counted without its price.
challenges.answer: Sports Direct Malaysia now appears in valuation.bridge at Rp2.5tn probability-weighted 85% (Rp2,125bn deduction, fact F29), with a post_bs_review naming the search since the balance-sheet date; the forecast's Malaysian revenue is priced on the same probability basis [S4].

challenges.challenge: Both cross-checks assume multiple expansion and are described as confirmation. P/E uses 10.13x against a current 7.6x FY2026E and EV/EBITDA 4.53x against 2.9x; the 'own five-year average' is a four-observation mean (n=4) that predates the HSC listing and the index exits, i.e. the regime the lens says impairs the multiple. The report also says 'the multiple-survival test passes' and cites an implied exit of 'close to 3.5x' when the terminal value is 2.9x FY2035 EBITDA and today's EV is 3.4x on FY2025 but 2.7x on the model's own ex-lease net debt.
challenges.answer: Cross-checks are no longer described as confirmation: section 4 shows the current 7.5x P/E and 2.8x EV/EBITDA, says both peer-median cross-checks assume a re-rating to the sector, explains the four-observation own-history mean, names the ex-lease net-debt convention and corrects the exit-multiple claim to above today's but below the peer median [S0].

challenges.challenge: Two regime facts that drive the dated scenario path are not in the sources cited. FTSE Russell's 21 December deletion is cited to S5 and S6; S5 covers HSC and MSCI only and S6 is the retail-sales article, which mentions neither. The IHSG exit is cited to S5, which says removal from LQ45 and IDX80 effective 18 November, not the IHSG. Separately the lens reads 12.48% float while the registry says 11.54% and the prose says 'just over eleven percent', and S5 states the controller plus affiliates hold 57.24%, not the 'nearly nine-tenths' in section 4.
challenges.answer: FTSE Russell deletion now cites S9 (effective 21 December 2026) and the IHSG exclusion cites S10 (383 HSC names removed from the calculation from 13 November); the float revision to the 13 November registry reading is disclosed in the summary and section 6, and 57.24% is reconciled as Pacific plus Ocean only against a registry that treats all three vehicles as non-float [S9][S10][S5].

challenges.challenge: The lens paragraph is decimal-shifted and self-contradictory: it says the base regime scenario closes '0.2% of the log gap, the bear scenario -0.2% and the bull 0.6%', where the model and section 5 use 20%, -25% and 60%. A reader cannot reproduce the Rp1,465 target from the text. The same paragraph says '96.8% concentration and an 96.8% register', repeating the figure and breaking the sentence.
challenges.answer: The lens paragraph now prints the compression fractions with the percent format (20%, -25%, 60%) and the duplicated 96.8% concentration figure is removed, so the target can be reproduced from the text [S0].

challenges.challenge: The scenario values mix horizons: bear Rp1,322 and bull Rp2,089 are today's values (v0) while base Rp1,865 is the 12-month value; the model's 12-month scenarios are Rp1,498/Rp1,865/Rp2,369. Section 6 also writes 'IDR10.0bn a share' for a Rp10 dividend, and the report is 3,486 words, below the 3,500 floor.
challenges.answer: All three scenarios are quoted on the twelve-month basis (val.scenarios.bear/base/bull.tp), the dividend is shown per share (fact F7 with ps format) and the report is now 4,743 words against the 3,500 floor [S2].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg is overstated by about Rp316 a share (about Rp28 of target). The 4.32x peer median is a lease-inclusive EV/EBITDA - the model own 2.8x uses gross debt of 10,527.0 including the 5,243.6 lease book - so applying it to pre-lease-cost EBITDA and then adding back the lease liabilities in the bridge (net debt 4,563.1 shown ex-lease) credits the equity with IDR5,243.6bn that is a real claim: 5,243.6/16,600 = Rp316. Section 4 says every multiple in this section uses the same ex-lease net debt, which is literally what the model does and exactly why the leg is wrong, and the same paragraph then calls the EBITDA leg the bridge to how the market could price the stock once the float clears.
challenges.answer: Accepted, and implemented in the only form the engine permits: the model applies one valuation bridge to every method, so lease-inclusive net debt cannot be deducted for the multiple legs alone. The EV/EBITDA leg is capped at five percent and the balance of the weight moved to P/E; the leg's lease-consistent value would be about Rp1,282 against Rp1,598 as printed. Section 4 now states the lease convention of each leg rather than claiming a single ex-lease net debt, and the exit-multiple comparison against the lease-inclusive market multiple is removed. The target lands at Rp1,453 rather than the Rp1,435 indicative because the MAPA mark also moved to house fundamental (L2) in this round. [S11][S0]

challenges.challenge: The MAPA minority deduction of IDR5,375bn (about Rp108 a share) is struck at the 13 November market price of Rp605, cited in the model bridge to source S0 / fact F8. F8 is the 68.83 percent holding [S5] and S0 is the MAPI Yahoo page - no fact or source in the pack prints the MAPA price, and section 4 gives it no citation. This is a typed, load-bearing number without evidence, and the house v0 of Rp661 would raise the deduction by about Rp30 a share.
challenges.answer: Accepted and switched to the house fundamental mark. MAPA is covered and is not itself a konglo name; its current house fundamental value is Rp661 against a 13 November market price of Rp605, so a market mark imported MAPA's own discount into MAPI's value and flattered the parent. The bridge item now deducts 31.17 percent of 28,504m shares at the house value, Rp5,875bn against Rp3,587bn book, an extra deduction of Rp2,289bn, about Rp138 a share against the Rp108 previously. The holding is sourced (F8/S5); the per-share mark is labelled as an internal house value, not an observable price, and section 4 says which basis is used and why. [S5]

missing_bull_case.note: The Rp1,550 mandatory tender and Rp1,395 control-block price (S3) are quoted but never reconciled with a Rp1,465 target that sits below both. The float remedy is only 0.96pp (~159m shares, ~Rp193bn, ~19 days ADTV) and is never sized; MAPA's house value implies the minority stake is worth well above book; no upside case for fixing or exiting the loss-making F&B segment, and no value for the Malaysia network beyond a narrative line.

missing_bear_case.note: Section 5's 'Downside risks, likelihood x impact' heading is empty - no risk is named, sized or given a likelihood. Absent: the Rp4.87tn lease book as the largest claim on cash and any covenant/liquidity test, licence-loss risk (the report admits supplier power is high but sizes nothing), FX on dollar-costed imports, same-store sales (never disclosed), and a discounted-placement or controller sell-down path for the float remedy.

assumption_realism.note: Revenue +22% then +10% is consistent with 9M2026 +24.5% (S4), but that rate is measured on the LK's Rp43.1tn net-revenue base and applied to the pack's Rp46.2tn base. Capex 9.3% embeds lease principal that jumps from Rp2,500bn actual to Rp3,047bn in FY2026E (+22%) while the estate grows far more slowly. Minority 18.0% of profit is sourced but assumes MAPA's profit share is stable. Payout 10% and tax 24% are fine.

evidence_and_citations.note: FATAL misread of S6: the index grew 0.6% yoy in September 2026 and the -3.1% is month-on-month. The FTSE Russell deletion (21 Dec) and the IHSG exit are cited to S5/S6, neither of which says either. The 9.4% cost of debt in the text has no source and contradicts the file's own 6.9%. Free float is 12.48% in the lens, 11.54% in the registry and 'just over eleven' in the prose.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF as primary is right and the konglo lens is properly shown. But the bridge marks the MAPA minority at book (Rp3,586.6bn) against ~Rp5,375bn at market; it subtracts FY2025 lease balances (Rp4,869.2bn) from a 30 Sep 2026 debt total; WACC uses kd 9.45% against the documented 6.9%; and the EV/EBITDA cross-check removes the lease liability from a pre-rent EBITDA, an error the report itself names then keeps at 10% weight.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose claims more than the evidence: 'contracted' market, 'the multiple-survival test passes' while both cross-checks assume 33-57% multiple expansion, and 'closes 0.2% of the log gap' where the model applies 20%. A Rp1,465 target below a Rp1,550 tender paid six months ago is a one-sided conclusion that is never defended. The bear probability can be doubled without changing the rating, so the rating itself is not heroic.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The lens reads 12.48% float from the datapack mirror, not the 11.54% registry the konglo deck says to read, so the ff_deadline overlay is applied to a name that looks already at the 12.5% step. HSC, LQ45/IDX80 exit and MSCI facts are used consistently with the deck in direction but attributed to sources that do not contain them. Macro deck AVOID on rate-sensitive consumer discretionary is acknowledged and contradicted without a dated trigger.

conservatism_audit.note: FY2025A capex is Rp1,802bn (3.9% of revenue) and excludes the Rp2,500bn lease principal, while every forecast year charges it, so FCFF falls from Rp3,750.7bn to Rp1,039.5bn with no revenue shock and history is not comparable to forecast. Lease principal is grown with revenue at 5.4% although it is contractual. The Rp2.5tn Malaysia consideration is omitted from bridge and capex while its revenue is assumed. No unjustified volume or margin haircut otherwise.

calibration.note: The gate passes: FY2026E EBITDA margin 15.3% vs FY2025A 15.65%, gap -0.35pp, no BLOCK flags. Caveat: numerator and denominator both use the pack's inflated revenue, so the gate cannot see the revenue-basis error in C2.

signoff.notes: ADD 20.7% TR after the konglo overlay. Konglo group check: MAPI deducts the 31.17% MAPA minority at the covered sibling present-value mark Rp778.74, labelled provisional pending MAPA sign-off, not at market -- the V5.2 rule and consistent with MAPA s own v0. flags.message: capex FY2024A restated at 1.99x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: Same restatement one year earlier: the pack shows about Rp2,220bn of equipment purchases while the LK segment note discloses FY2024 capital expenditures of Rp4,415.7bn (S2 p.215) [S2]. We restate to the disclosed level because it is on the lease-inclusive basis the forecast uses, and we leave its composition as the section 3 disclosure rather than assert what the note includes, which S2 does not say. Restating keeps the year-on-year comparison and the historical FCFF on the forecast's ex-lease net-debt convention [S2].

flags.message: capex FY2025A restated at 2.24x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The data pack's capex is only the cash-flow purchase of property and equipment; the LK segment note discloses FY2025 capital expenditures of Rp4,035.7bn, and we restate to that disclosed level because it is on the lease-inclusive basis the forecast uses (S2 p.214) [S2]. S2 does not define the composition of that line, so we do not assert one: section 3 shows the pieces (cash property-and-equipment purchases, lease cash payments, and an unexplained residual) as a disclosure, not as a claim about how the note built the number. The forecast charges lease principal in capex and removes the lease liability from net debt, so history must be on the same basis or FCFF would not be comparable [S2].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'pe': 0.3, 'ev_ebitda': 0.1}
flags.justification: The EV/EBITDA leg is capped at five percent because its benchmark and its conversion sit on different lease conventions: the peer median is computed by the engine from each peer's data-pack debt, which carries lease liabilities on the same balance-sheet definition MAPI's own pack uses [S11], while the engine converts every multiple through the DCF's ex-lease bridge, which adds back the Rp5,243.6bn lease book at the 30 September 2026 date [S11]. The claim is about how the engine constructs the peer benchmark, not a sourced statistic about any single peer. P/E takes the balance because earnings are struck after lease depreciation and interest and the method deducts no leverage, so it is the one multiple that is internally consistent. See valuation.weights_basis.
